clips.send: Oracle-bone script. Late Shang dynasty, c. 1300–1046 BCE. Kings asked their ancestors questions — “Will it rain?” “Will the hunt go well?” — and scribes carved the answers on bones. Found in 1899; most come from Yinxu (殷墟) near Anyang, Henan. About 4,500 different characters have been found; only around a third can be read so far. Very picture-like, and not fixed: a character could face left or right.

clips.send: Forbidden City. Palace of the Ming and Qing emperors, finished in 1420; today the Palace Museum 24 Ming and Qing emperors lived here. It covers about 720,000 square meters — the largest and most complete ancient palace complex still standing in the world, held together by wooden joints instead of nails.

clips.send: Bronze script. Shang and Zhou dynasties. Written in the clay mould, then cast into bronze ritual vessels — so the strokes look thick and soft. The Mao Gong Ding (毛公鼎), a Western Zhou cauldron, carries nearly 500 characters — the longest bronze inscription known. Still picture-like, but more regular than oracle bones.

clips.send: Regular script. Formed by the Wei–Jin era, perfected in the Tang. 楷 means “model”: every stroke clear and separate — the script children learn first. Tang masters: Ouyang Xun (欧阳询), Yan Zhenqing (颜真卿), Liu Gongquan (柳公权). Since 1956 mainland China uses simplified characters (简化字), e.g. 馬, 马.

clips.send: Small seal script. Qin dynasty, 221 BCE. After Qin Shi Huang united China he ordered “one script for all” (书同文). Chancellor Li Si (李斯) helped set the standard. Round, even lines of the same thickness; tall rectangular shapes. Example: the stone inscription on Mount Tai (《泰山刻石》).

clips.send: Clerical script. Qin–Han dynasties (most used in the Han). Busy government clerks needed speed: round curves became straight, square strokes. This change is called 隶变 (lìbiàn). 隶变 is the great divide between ancient characters and modern characters — from here you can read most characters! Wide, flat shapes; horizontal strokes start like a silkworm’s head and end like a swallow’s tail (蚕头燕尾).

clips.send: 楷书。汉末魏晋形成，唐代达到高峰。“楷”是楷模、规范的意思，笔画清楚，横平竖直。。唐代楷书大家：欧阳询、颜真卿、柳公权。。1956年起，中国大陆推行简化字，如“馬”简化为“马”。

clips.send: 故宫。明清两代的皇宫，1420年建成；今天是故宫博物院 明清两代共有24位皇帝住在这里。故宫占地约72万平方米，是世界上现存规模最大、最完整的古代宫殿建筑群，大殿主要靠榫卯连接，不用钉子。

clips.send: 甲骨文。商朝后期（约公元前1300—前1046年）。商王用龟甲兽骨占卜（“会下雨吗？”“打猎顺利吗？”），把占卜的事刻在上面。。1899年被发现，大多出土于河南安阳殷墟。。已发现单字约4500个，能释读的约三分之一。。象形程度高，写法不固定，方向可左可右。

clips.send: 金文。商周时期。先写在泥范上，再铸到青铜礼器上，所以笔画粗壮丰满。。西周毛公鼎铭文近500字，是现存最长的青铜器铭文。。仍有图画味，但比甲骨文规整。

clips.send: 小篆。秦朝（公元前221年统一文字）。秦始皇统一六国后“书同文”，丞相李斯等整理出小篆作为标准字体。。线条圆转，粗细均匀，字形长方。。代表：《泰山刻石》。

clips.send: 泰山。五岳之首；杜甫《望岳》（约736年） 泰山在今山东，海拔1545米，古代帝王在这里祭天。杜甫望着它，立志“会当凌绝顶，一览众山小”。

clips.send: 隶书。秦汉时期，通行于汉代。为了书写方便，小篆的圆转线条变成了平直方折的笔画，这叫“隶变”。。隶变是古文字和今文字的分水岭，从隶书开始，汉字大多能认出来了。。字形扁方，横画“蚕头燕尾”。代表：东汉《曹全碑》（185年）。
